issue: Latin tag rendered "will-o'-the-wisp"; source "this ignis fatuus in finance"; STYLE-NOTE keeps Latin tags as printed.
replacement: What remedy can there be for this situation, except a change of the system that produced it, a change of the false and deceptive system of quotas and requisitions? What substitute can be imagined for this ignis fatuus in finance, other than permitting the national government to raise its own revenues by the ordinary methods of taxation authorized in every well-ordered constitution of civil government? Ingenious men may argue plausibly on any subject, but no human ingenuity can point out any other expedient to rescue us from the problems and embarrassments that naturally result from an inadequately supplied public treasury.

issue: Source "an opposite interest prevailed"; candidate "a different interest" weakens opposition.
replacement: To argue from abstract principles that this coordinate authority cannot exist is to set supposition and theory against fact and reality. Such reasoning may be proper for showing that a thing OUGHT NOT TO EXIST. It must be wholly rejected when it is used to prove that a thing does not exist, in the face of the fact itself. It is well known that in the Roman republic the legislative authority, in the last resort, rested for ages in two different political bodies. They were not branches of one legislature but distinct and independent legislatures, and in each an opposing interest prevailed: the patrician in one, the plebeian in the other. Many arguments might have been offered to prove that two such seemingly contradictory authorities, each able to ANNUL or REPEAL the acts of the other, were unfit to coexist. But anyone at Rome who tried to disprove their existence would have been thought frantic. It will be readily understood that I am referring to the COMITIA CENTURIATA and the COMITIA TRIBUTA. In the former, where the people voted by centuries, the arrangement gave the patrician interest the advantage. In the latter, where numbers prevailed, the plebeian interest was wholly predominant. And yet these two legislatures existed side by side for ages, and the Roman republic rose to the utmost height of human greatness.

issue: Source "the probable duration of the world"; candidate drops "probable".
replacement: To judge the true merits of this question more precisely, it will be well to look at the proportion between the objects that will require a federal provision of revenue and those that will require a State provision. We shall find that the former are altogether unlimited and the latter are held within very moderate bounds. In pursuing this inquiry we must keep in mind that we are not to look only at the present period but forward to a remote future. Constitutions of civil government are not to be framed on a calculation of present necessities alone, but on a combination of these with the probable necessities of ages, following the natural and tried course of human affairs. Nothing, therefore, can be more fallacious than to infer, from an estimate of its immediate necessities, how much power ought to be lodged in the national government. There ought to be a CAPACITY to provide for future contingencies as they arise; and since these are illimitable by nature, it is impossible to limit that capacity safely. It is true, perhaps, that one could compute, accurately enough for the purpose, how much revenue is needed to discharge the Union's existing engagements and to maintain the peacetime establishments that would suffice for some time to come. But would it be wise, or would it not rather be the extreme of folly, to stop at this point? That would leave the government entrusted with the national defense wholly incapable of protecting the community against future breaches of the public peace, whether by foreign war or domestic convulsions. If, on the contrary, we ought to go past this point, where can we stop short of an indefinite power to provide for emergencies as they arise? It is easy to assert, in general terms, that a rational judgment can be formed of a proper provision against probable dangers. But we may safely challenge those who make this assertion to produce their data, and may affirm that those data would prove as vague and uncertain as any that could be offered to establish how long the world will probably last. Observations confined to the mere prospect of internal attacks deserve no weight, though even these admit of no satisfactory calculation. And if we mean to be a commercial people, our policy must include being able one day to defend that commerce. Supporting a navy and naval wars would involve contingencies that must defeat all the efforts of political arithmetic.

issue: Added hedge: source "will always be inclined, with few exceptions"; candidate "will almost always be inclined, with few exceptions". Also (NIT): Source "more equal to a contest with any spirit"; candidate "better able to face down" adds connotation of intimidation.
replacement: The idea of actual representation of all classes of the people by persons from each class is altogether visionary. Unless the Constitution expressly provided that each different occupation should send one or more members, the thing would never happen in practice. Mechanics and manufacturers will always be inclined, with few exceptions, to vote for merchants rather than for persons of their own professions or trades. These discerning citizens are well aware that the mechanic and manufacturing arts furnish the materials of mercantile enterprise and industry. Many of them, indeed, are directly connected with the operations of commerce. They know that the merchant is their natural patron and friend. They know that, however much confidence they may rightly have in their own good sense, the merchant can advance their interests more effectively than they can themselves. They are aware that their habits in life have not given them those acquired endowments without which, in a deliberative assembly, the greatest natural abilities are for the most part useless. And they are aware that the influence, weight and superior acquirements of the merchants make them better able to contend with any spirit that might happen to find its way into the public councils unfriendly to the manufacturing and trading interests. These considerations, and many others that might be mentioned, prove, and experience confirms, that artisans and manufacturers will commonly be disposed to give their votes to merchants and to those whom the merchants recommend. We must therefore consider merchants the natural representatives of all these classes of the community.

issue: Garbled rendering of "moderate proprietors of land": candidate "owners of moderate land".
replacement: Nothing remains but the landed interest. In a political view, and particularly with respect to taxes, I take this to be perfectly united, from the wealthiest landlord down to the poorest tenant. No tax can be laid on land that will not affect the owner of millions of acres just as it affects the owner of a single acre. Every landholder will therefore share an interest in keeping the taxes on land as low as possible, and common interest can always be counted on as the surest bond of sympathy. But even if we could suppose a difference of interest between the wealthy landholder and the middling farmer, what reason is there to conclude that the first would have a better chance than the last of being sent to the national legislature? If we take fact as our guide and look at our own senate and assembly, we shall find that moderate landowners prevail in both. This is no less true in the senate, which has fewer members, than in the assembly, which has more. Where the qualifications of the electors are the same, whether they have to choose a small number or a large one, their votes will go to those in whom they have most confidence, whether these happen to be men of large fortunes, of moderate property, or of no property at all.
